newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Wu urges Pakistan not to scrap $5.5 bln power deal.
newsitem.headline: Wu urges Pakistan not to scrap $5.5 bln power deal.

text.p: Hong Kong-based tycoon Gordon Wu said on Friday that Pakistan had no justification for its declared plans to scrap a $5.5 billion power project to be built by his Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd (CEPA).

"There are no grounds for the government or WAPDA (the state-owned Water and Power Development Authority) to terminate the project," Wu said in a statement. "A failure to honour the agreements (with Pakistan and WAPDA) would clearly send the wrong message to the international investment community."

Wu said CEPA had not received any notice to terminate the project to construct a power plant comprising eight 660-megawatt coal-fired thermal power units at Keti Bandar, about 60 km (37 miles) west of Karachi, in the southern province of Sindh.

Water and Power Minister Nisar Ali Khan told the National Assembly (lower house) last week that the government had decided to terminate the deal because the cost of electricity from CEPA would exceed $0.11 per kilowatt hour.
Khan later told Reuters the government would seek to terminate the deal with CEPA "by mutual agreement".
CEPA, in which U.S. power giant Southern Co has an 80 percent stake and Hong Kong's Hopewell Holdings Ltd 20 percent, contests Khan's projection of the electricity cost.
"The cost of electricity at Keti Bandar under the power purchase agreement is an average of 4.738 U.S. cents over 30 years, or a levelised tariff of 5.578 U.S. cents over the same period," Wu said.

He said the minister's price tag for electricity from the CEPA power plant included the cost of delivery from Keti Bandar to WAPDA's grid station at Jamshoro via a 185-km (116-mile) transmission line that has yet to be built.
Wu said Pakistan should tender for construction of the transmission line project to determine what impact it would have on the cost of electricity.

"The minister's estimate that the 185-km transmission line would more than double the cost of electricity assumes that bids from private sector transmission companies to construct the line would be a substantial order of magnitude higher than previous quotes received by the government of Pakistan for other similar projects," Wu argued.
"Alternatively, CEPA has offered to construct the transmission line at a much lower cost," he added.

CEPA said last week it had awarded a $1.8-billion construction contract to a Japanese-American consortium and bought 3,000 acres (1,200 hectares) of land from the Sindh provincial government for the project.
"Work continues on site preparation at the power station site and a great deal of effort and money has been spent to date," Wu said.

"CEPA remains committed to Pakistan and the Keti Bandar project and sincerely hopes that the new government will see the benefit in a project which promises to be a large reliable source of affordable electricity, and the largest foreign investment in Pakistan to date," he said.
Under the agreement, CEPA was to build the first two power units to operate on imported coal while the remainder would use coal from the Thar fields in Sindh, if this proved feasible.
CEPA also had plans to develop a 14-metre (43-foot) deep sea port in Sindh and set up a special industrial zone at the site at a total cost of $1.0 billion.
